articleTitle: Stormwater Management via Infiltration Park for Community Resilience
abstract: Climate change-induced extreme weather events threaten aging water management systems. Flooding and surface runoff occurs when these systems are overwhelmed, posing risks to life, property, and water quality. Low-income and disadvantaged communities are particularly vulnerable to extreme weather events. These communities receive less investment in maintaining and updating their water management systems, increasing susceptibility to floods. Additionally, disadvantaged communities are more likely to be near pollutant sources. The lack of investment and increased pollution risk leaves low-income communities with an urgent need for solutions, but limited resources. A cost-efficient solution to implement in disadvantaged communities must be developed to sustainably manage stormwater and decrease the likelihood of flooding. Here, the Infiltration Park for Community Resilience was designed for implementation on an undeveloped 15,000 square meter lot in the City of San Joaquin, in the Central Valley of California, USA. The City of San Joaquin is a small community with a 33% poverty rate and an average household income of $59,000 [1] [2]. This community also has a very high flood risk to homes and other structures (all structures are at risk of flooding in the next 30 years) [3]. After selection of San Joaquin for site development, several stormwater management solutions were researched and evaluated based on how well they met the design requirements. Bioswales, green roofs, wetland parks, and more were evaluated on criteria such as cost consideration and passive treatment capabilities. Elements of rain gardens, infiltration basins and bioswales were incorporated into the full-scale design. The focal point of the design is the infiltration basin. The basin encourages stormwater infiltration, preventing flooding and replenishing the groundwater aquifer. Biosorption activated media, which is very effective at removing sediments and pollutants that make stormwater difficult to manage, will be layered beneath the basin to improve the passive treatment capabilities of the basin. Rain gardens will be implemented throughout the park to slow stormwater flows, encourage groundwater infiltration, and passively treat stormwater while increasing biodiversity and aesthetic appeal of the park. The bench-scale model and full-scale projections indicated that the park design would help infiltrate and retain up to 10% of the entire City of San Joaquin's stormwater runoff in a 100-year storm. Consequently, this infiltration park would lighten the load placed on the stormwater system during extreme weather events and lessen the extent of flooding damage to the city. The infiltration park offers many community benefits in addition to its role as a piece of stormwater infrastructure--the park will provide much needed greenspace for the community. The playground, picnic tables, and walking paths will encourage community members to enjoy the space and add physical exercise to their routine.

articleTitle: Purifying Salt Water Disposal Well Water for Green Hydrogen Production
abstract: The treatment system detailed in this report treats produced water from fracking to deionized-quality (DI-quality) standards for hydrogen energy production. Hydrogen has been determined to be a promising clean energy source due to its high energy density. Produced water has been determined as a possible source of DI-quality water because of its high energy potential. It exits the wellhead at a high temperature and pressure which allows for innovative treatment options utilizing these unique conditions. The bench-scale system implements biochar adsorption, membrane distillation (MD), and capacitive deionization (CDI) to remove TrueSyn oil, Sodium Bentonite Drilling Clay, Arizona Test Dust, and Sodium Chloride from the inlet stream. The full-scale design utilizes turbines for power generation, oil/water separation, biochar filtration, MD, and CDI to remove colloidal matter, oil, dust, and salt from the solution. Preliminary data from the bench-scale model supports process applicability with a final turbidity of 0.40 ppm and a final measurable conductivity of 6 μS/cm.

articleTitle: Combined Physisorption and Electrochemistry System for Modular Direct CO2 Capture and Storage
abstract: Scientists agree that isolated changes to the energy grid are insufficient to mitigate many detrimental impacts of anthropogenic climate change on human and ecological health. Novel, sustainable, and modular carbon dioxide removal (CDR) technologies offer options to mitigate impacts. The proposed direct air capture (DAC) system pairs physisorption in a zeolite-packed bed reactor with electrochemistry to precipitate and store captured carbon dioxide (CO<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</inf>) as calcium carbonate (CaCO<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">3</inf>). The sorption column produces an outlet stream 2,230 times more concentrated than ambient air, with a CO<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</inf> concentration of 94.7%. This CO<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</inf>-rich stream is fed into the cathode chamber of an electrochemical cell, which is filled with hard membrane filtration reject water. The electrochemical cell maintains an alkaline pH, allowing the gaseous CO<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</inf>-rich stream to dissolve in the high hardness solution and form carbonate ions. Carbonate ions react with calcium ions present in the solution to form CaC0<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">3</inf>. Bench scale testing has resulted in qualitative evidence of CaCO<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">3</inf> formation. The system generates no waste during operation, and CaCO<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">3</inf> is a stable, nontoxic solid which can persist indefinitely at ambient conditions. Based on the bench-scale model, the full-scale design removes 131 gross tons of CO<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</inf> from ambient air every year, recovering the CO<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</inf> emitted during technology construction, operation, and ultimate decommissioning over a 30-year lifetime. Seven modules, each consisting of 100 adsorption columns and two electrochemical cells, capture 100 net tons of CO<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</inf> annually.

articleTitle: Stormwater Management for Environmental and Climate Justice Community Resilience
abstract: This study presents a comprehensive approach to sustainable stormwater management in disadvantaged urban areas, focusing on New Orleans' neighborhood of the Lower 9<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">th</sup> Ward. The goal is to address environmental concerns such as flooding and contamination while taking into consideration what improvements can be made in the community. Through collaboration with local organizations, an innovative design was developed to incorporate modern technologies and materials to mitigate flooding, improve water quality, and provide co-benefits to the community. This design, as a modular unit, features tree filter systems and a bioretention basin placed in accordance with natural hydrology to slow and treat stormwater runoff before it enters the city's drainage system. Laboratory testing was conducted to evaluate the efficiency of various media selected to treat the contamination found on site through soil and water sampling.

articleTitle: Conversion of Sodium Sulfate Using Bipolar Membrane Electrodialysis for a Circular Economy
abstract: Every year, two to four million tons of sodium sulfate is extracted as a manufacturing byproduct. Common disposal pathways include placement in solid waste landfills, subsurface disposal, or the ocean. Developing new methodologies to reuse this byproduct in the factories that generate sodium sulfate or other upstream processes promotes environmental sustainability and a circular economy. This paper explores bipolar membrane electrodialysis (BMED) as a viable option for sodium sulfate reuse. A 3D printed continuous loop bipolar membrane electrodialysis cell was used to turn aqueous sodium sulfate into sulfuric acid and sodium hydroxide.

articleTitle: Stormwater Management in Cold Climates: A Green Solution for Salinity Reduction
abstract: The escalation of extreme wet weather events driven by climate change impacts both the quantity and quality of water, putting communities with outdated infrastructure and limited resources at a disadvantage. The implementation of bioretention cells, bioswales, and check dams will mitigate the effects of extreme wet weather events in Dollar Bay, MI, a disadvantaged community located in the northern United States that receives a high rate of snowfall at 206 inches per year. Rain-on-snow events will affect Dollar Bay resulting in flooding during the spring snowmelt. Another issue cold-climate communities like Dollar Bay experience are high salinity levels in the watershed due to road salts used in the winter. The cells will be modified to reduce salinity in urban runoff through the addition of biochar and kaolin clay to the soil. The green infrastructure design, modeled using ArcGIS Pro, HEC-HMS, and EPA SWMM, will reduce 69% of runoff in a 100-yr storm event, and reduce the peak flow velocity by 66%. Bench-scale testing utilizing a soil mix of 2% biochar and 5% kaolin clay confirmed 100% salinity reduction. Overall, the stormwater design not only decreases the risk of flooding and salinity concentrations in runoff, but also implements green space and provides economic and societal benefits for residents, appealing to all aspects of the triple bottom line of sustainability.

articleTitle: Sodium Sulfate Salt Splitting for Sulfuric Acid and Sodium Hydroxide Production
abstract: Sodium sulfate is produced as a by-product in several chemical processes, including the water recovery plant at Freeport-McMoRan Inc. (FMI). Sodium sulfate has many applications, but an economically viable product cannot currently be produced by FMI, resulting in their sodium sulfate being transported as waste to a landfill. We aim to utilize electrolysis to produce and recycle sulfuric acid and sodium hydroxide back to the FMI plant and, in turn, reduce waste production and transportation fees.

articleTitle: PyBIG-Enhanced Liquid Sorbent Direct Air Capture
abstract: The pressing need to combat climate change and transition towards a more sustainable future demands the implementation of carbon capture technology. Anthropogenic carbon dioxide has accumulated in the atmosphere since the industrial revolution, inducing adverse climate change effects. Current atmospheric CO<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</inf> must be removed to avoid rising sea levels, low agricultural productivity, and high-frequency extreme weather events. Carbon dioxide removal (CDR) technologies like direct air capture (DAC) have proved challenging due to CO<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</inf>'S low atmospheric concentration of 421 ppm and have remained economically unfeasible at industrial scale. Current DAC systems rely on technologies such as liquid sorbent media, membrane filtration, and/or solid adsorbent media. These technologies were evaluated against each other, and a modified liquid sorbent media process was selected as the best available design. This process is enhanced by adding an amino guanidine compound 2,6-pyridine-bis(aminoguanidine) (PyBIG) in an intermediate crystallization step which lowers energy inputs and improves sorbent regeneration. Research was conducted to develop an improved method for sustainable, efficient, and economically viable modular direct air carbon capture using PyBIG. Although DAC includes two steps-atmospheric capture and long-term storage of CO<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</inf>-the scope of the research only included enhancement of the capture process, specifically researching the previous challenges of PyBIG utilization, and integrating PyBIG into an autonomous CDR module.

articleTitle: Threefold CO2 Removal for a Cleaner Tomorrow
abstract: In response to the ever-growing threat of climate change driven by human activities, this study presents a modular approach to carbon capture, targeting community-level implementation. Multiple promising methods are explored throughout the paper but ultimately were unattainable for the paper's research such as sequestration through concrete and oysters, bamboo, algae, and shellfish. Through a combination of methods including a liquid metal catalyst reaction, biochar production, and basalt dust mineralization, the aim is to remove 100 tons of CO<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</inf> from the atmosphere annually. To reach the removal goal, around five modules would need to be implemented throughout the nation. The liquid-metal catalyst reaction is an incredible demonstration to help educate the public and would capture less than one ton annually. For the biochar portion of the study, a pyrolysis oven was used to generate biochar using leaves, sticks, grass, etc. by reducing oxygen and using high temperatures to convert the biogenic carbon to biochar. The calculations show that if there were approximately 30 trees per acre in a 10.5-acre park, 13.9 tons of CO<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</inf> would be captured. The basalt portion of the study uses basalt dust to remove CO<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</inf> from the atmosphere. Each module will use two tons of basalt over five acres to remove 7.42 tons of CO<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</inf> annually.
